title: MemRL: Self-Evolving Agents via Runtime Reinforcement Learning on Episodic Memory
claim: Learning systems can mirror human episodic memory by keeping the reasoner frozen while a plastic memory evolves through feedback.
layout: 2 panels left-to-right joined by a big arrow, brain-to-robot analogy
description: The figure has two panels joined by a large pink arrow. The left panel, on a warm beige background, is titled 'Human cognition'. It shows a thought cloud with an 'Intent' node linking to note cards that lead to an 'expected outcome', plus a green 'update expected outcome' tag with a wrench. Below the cloud is a brain with a lock icon, and an 'Episodic memory' box holds a stack: episode, expected outcome, strategy. The arrow in the middle reads 'Inspired by constructive episodic simulation: Decouple stable reasoning from plastic episode memory', with a lightbulb. The right panel, titled 'MemRL (runtime learning)', shows a robot whose body holds a locked, frozen LLM and a memory jar with intent, solution attempt and utility score entries. Arrows lead to the environment and feedback, and 'Value-aware retrieval' links back. The right side of the panel is cropped. Pastel purples, greens and pinks dominate.
caption: The conceptual framework of MemRL.
abstract: The hallmark of human intelligence is the self-evolving ability to master new skills by learning from past experiences. However, current AI agents struggle to emulate this self-evolution: fine-tuning is computationally expensive and prone to catastrophic forgetting, while existing memory-based methods rely on passive semantic matching that often retrieves noise. To address these challenges, we propose MemRL, a non-parametric approach that evolves via reinforcement learning on episodic memory. By decoupling stable reasoning from plastic memory, MemRL employs a Two-Phase Retrieval mechanism to filter noise and identify high-utility strategies through environmental feedback. Extensive experiments on HLE, BigCodeBench, ALFWorld, and Lifelong Agent Bench demonstrate that MemRL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, confirming that MemRL effectively reconciles the stability-plasticity dilemma, enabling continuous runtime improvement without weight updates. Code is available at https://github.com/MemTensor/MemRL.
